prompt.context: Your client is a large agricultural equipment manufacturer. Their primary product line, farming tractors, is losing money.
prompt.question: What questions would you ask of your client to help them solve their profitability problem?

clarifying_info.a: Your client has 40% of the market, competitor #1: 30%, competitor #2: 15%, remaining 15% belongs to many small manufacturers. Five years ago, your client had 60%, competitor #1: 15%, competitor #2: 10%.

clarifying_info.q: Do all three competitors sell to the same customers?
Is your client's product priced differently from competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Your client's product is priced higher than the others, and this has always been the case.

clarifying_info.q: Are the products essentially the same?
clarifying_info.a: Essentially yes, they all have the same basic features. Of course, tractors are not commodity items and a few differences do exist.

clarifying_info.q: What differences allow the client to charge a premium?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a strong reputation/image of quality. The market has always been willing to pay a premium for that reputation because it meant tractors would last longer and need less maintenance, which is critical for farmers who can't afford equipment breakdown at a critical time.

clarifying_info.q: Are sales revenues down? Are sales quantities down?
Is the price down? Are all costs the same?
clarifying_info.a: No. In fact both the price and costs are up.
No. Material costs (variable costs) have gone up significantly, and the client has no answer as to why material prices have gone up so much.

clarifying_info.q: Do you manufacture or just assemble?
Have finished part prices gone up?
Have raw material prices for your suppliers gone up?
Have labor costs increased for your suppliers?
Why are your suppliers charging higher prices for the same product?
clarifying_info.a: They are not charging for the same product — prices have increased as a result of the client's own product improvement efforts. The client has tightened tolerances and improved the durability of component parts.

clarifying_info.q: Why do you make these improvements?
clarifying_info.a: Because we strive to continue to sell the best tractors in the world.

clarifying_info.q: Are your customers willing to pay for these product improvements?
clarifying_info.a: Unknown. The client assumes they will, but has not verified this.

framework: Understand the competitive landscape: number of competitors, market share, pricing positioning
Diagnose revenue decline: price trends, volume trends, customer segments
Diagnose cost increases: fixed vs. variable costs, supply chain analysis (raw materials, labor, supplier relationships)
Identify root cause of cost inflation: product improvement decisions and their cost impact
Assess customer value perception: willingness to pay for incremental improvements
Evaluate strategic alignment: whether product improvement investments are justified by customer demand

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the profitability problem?
questions.guidance: A strong answer traces the issue through two linked mechanisms: (1) market share has fallen from 60% to 40% over five years while competitor share grew, indicating customers are switching away despite (or because of) higher prices; (2) variable (material) costs have risen because the client has been tightening tolerances and improving component durability on its own initiative, raising supplier costs which are passed through. Prices were raised to cover these costs, but customers do not value the improvements enough to pay the higher price, so volumes declined further.

questions.prompt: Has the client been conducting a cost/benefit analysis on its product improvement process?
questions.guidance: The answer is no. The client has been assuming customers will pay for improvements, but has not validated this. The improvements add cost but customers either do not notice the improvement or do not value it enough to pay the premium, causing volume loss.

brainstorming.prompt: What questions should a consultant ask to fully diagnose the profitability problem of the agricultural equipment manufacturer?

categories.name: Competitive Landscape
ideas: How many competitors exist and what are their market shares?
Has market share shifted over time?
Do competitors sell to the same customer segments?
How does competitor pricing compare?

categories.name: Revenue Analysis
ideas: Are revenues down due to price decreases or volume decreases?
Which customer segments are leaving?
Is the price premium still justified by brand reputation?

categories.name: Cost Analysis
ideas: Have fixed costs changed?
Have variable/material costs changed?
Has the supplier base changed?
Have raw material or labor costs at suppliers changed?

categories.name: Product & Operations
ideas: Is this a manufacturing or assembly operation?
Have finished component prices increased?
Has the product specification changed?
Who authorized changes to component tolerances?

categories.name: Customer Value
ideas: Are customers aware of the product improvements?
Are customers willing to pay for the improvements?
Has customer feedback been solicited on recent changes?
Do farmers value durability improvements enough to pay a premium?

categories.name: Strategic Process
ideas: Does the client have a formal cost/benefit process for product changes?
Are product improvement decisions linked to customer research?
What is the long-term brand strategy if the premium is eroded?

recommendation: The client must implement a cost/benefit analysis procedure into its product improvement process before approving changes that raise component costs

Prices raised to cover unapproved improvements should be evaluated against actual customer willingness to pay — improvements customers do not value should be rolled back or absorbed without a price increase
The client should investigate whether its shrinking market share (60% to 40% over five years) can be reversed by repricing or by communicating the value of its quality improvements more effectively
risks: Rolling back improvements may damage the quality reputation that underpins the client's pricing premium
If competitors adopt similar improvements later at lower cost, the client could lose its differentiation advantage
Long-term effects of cost-cutting on product durability could harm the brand if equipment reliability declines
next_steps: Conduct customer research to quantify willingness to pay for specific product improvements
Audit recent component specification changes and calculate their cost impact
Build a stage-gate process requiring customer validation before product improvements are approved
Analyze whether the 20-point market share loss is recoverable and at what price point
